title: First Guest
subtitle: Comparing Means Assignment · t-test, ANOVA, pairwise tests
story: You own Calmarupe, the old bathhouse cut into the sea cliff at the foot of the city. The first snow fell in the night; now it is dawn, the morning after, and every roof above is white. Diana Volpe, your fiercest rival, is already boarding the funicular at the harbour with her friends: the first guests of the day, and the last people you want to find a single flaw. Certify the water in every bath before her car reaches the clifftop at sunrise: the cold plunge, the brine cave, the warm hall, then the springs on the clifftop terrace. You start in the dim entry hall at the waterline, where two bell-cords hang by the hidden stair — old servants' bells whose ropes climb through the rock to the bell tower on the clifftop. Today they will do something stranger.

done.title: The house reads true
done.body: Every bath, certified — cold plunge to clifftop spring, nothing out of balance and nothing for Diana to find. Now to be gone before she steps off the funicular.

escapeDone.title: First tracks
escapeDone.body: The five candles burn in their pattern and the tower door swings open. You step out onto the clifftop walk beside the aqueduct, the snow untouched, just as the funicular docks at the terrace below — flawless, and first. Let her follow.

debrief.title: How Calmarupe worked
debrief.intro: Every room asked the question a bath-keeper asks each morning: is this difference real, or just the wobble of water? You certified each bath by choosing the honest test for its data, and the springs by refusing to cry wolf on every pool after the snow. Here is how each room embodied the comparison of means.

entry.title: The bell tower
entry.text: Every bath certified, honestly — nothing for Diana to find. The sun strikes the bell tower above the terrace; up in the belfry, beneath the five bells, five balance-candles stand dark. Go back, read each pair of candles, and pull the right cords.

rooms.debrief: No console in the belfry — just your eye. All morning you asked whether a difference was real; here you ask it of candlelight. A pair whose candles are plainly one massive, one tiny truly differ — pull that colour's cord and light its candle; a pair whose candles all match does not — leave it dark. Recognising that, then finding each colour's cord a room behind, is the whole comparison made physical.
